extracted.intended_audience: early-career researchers (ECRs) submitting manuscripts to academic journals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for early-career researchers on how to reduce the chance a submitted manuscript is rejected by an editor without peer review, by addressing novelty, scope, methods, writing, ethics, and targeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak novelty or contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts that do not offer something fresh — a new method, new population focus, novel interpretation, or conceptual advance — risk being dismissed early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors assess whether a paper 'moves the conversation forward' by posing a compelling research question, offering a distinct conceptual angle, or challenging prevailing assumptions. Novelty can be theoretical innovation, methodological advancement, or empirical discovery (especially in underexplored contexts). Explicitly state the unique contribution in the cover letter, introduction (gap statement), and discussion; do not assume editors will 'see' the novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Out of scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting to a journal whose aims and readership do not align with the topic often leads to immediate desk rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read the journal's 'Aims and Scope' and review the types of studies it has published recently. Consider whether the audience (clinical, global health, nutrition, public health, etc.) matches your manuscript. Tailor framing and language to fit the target journal rather than submitting blindly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor alignment with journal standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts that are too localized, descriptive, or programmatic and do not offer broader insights or generalizable lessons may fail to meet a journal's threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study recent articles and editorial expectations for the target journal. High-impact journals expect manuscripts that go beyond describing events and instead offer broader implications, innovations, or transferable lessons. Authors should compare their manuscript’s scope and ambition to what the journal typically publishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Flawed or poorly explained study design, sampling, measurement, or analysis will prompt editors to reject without peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-plan sample size with power calculations, use validated instruments, clearly describe methods, and anticipate weaknesses in the Methods or Limitations sections. Apply recognized reporting standards (e.g., STROBE, CONSORT, PRISMA) to demonstrate rigor and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor writing and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusing prose, grammatical errors, and poor structure make manuscripts time-consuming to fix and can lead to desk rejection despite strong science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, direct English and a clear IMRAD structure (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion). Run grammar/clarity checkers (e.g., Grammarly, Hemingway), ask colleagues for feedback, or use professional editing. Prepare a one-page outline before writing to ensure logical flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical or reporting concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Missing documentation of ethical approval, unclear conflict-of-interest declarations, or absent funding disclosures are serious issues that can block review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State Institutional Review Board or ethical committee approval (with reference numbers where available), mention informed consent (or guardian consent for minors), and disclose funding sources and conflicts of interest (or explicitly state none). Create a pre-submission checklist for ethics approval ✓ consent ✓ funding ✓ conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Too early-stage or narrow analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies presenting baseline data, preliminary findings, or exploratory surveys without sufficient analysis or synthesis may not yet be ready for journal publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors favour complete, mature studies that tell a compelling scientific story. If your work is preliminary, strengthen analysis, interpretation, and the broader implications before submission or choose a more appropriate venue for early-stage work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target journals carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing an appropriate journal whose aims, scope, and readership match your manuscript reduces the risk of desk rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study 2–3 potential journals: read 'Aims and Scope', review types of studies published in the last two years, and consider audience. Use tools like Jane Journal Finder or Elsevier Journal Finder and consult mentors or colleagues. Tailor manuscript framing and cover letter language to the chosen journal; never submit blindly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reporting standards and plan design rigorously
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensuring methodological rigor and adherence to reporting standards increases the likelihood editors will send the paper for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-plan sample sizes (power calculations), use validated instruments, and follow reporting guidelines appropriate to the study type (STROBE for observational, CONSORT for trials, PRISMA for reviews). Include a paragraph explaining why the design is appropriate and proactively address anticipated reviewer concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize and state novelty explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the manuscript's original contribution obvious to editors rather than assuming they'll infer it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the cover letter, briefly state what makes the research original and why it matters. End the Introduction with a clear 'gap statement' (e.g., 'To our knowledge, no prior studies have examined...'). In the Discussion, highlight advances to science, policy implications, and new avenues for inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish writing and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear, concise, and well-organized writing is essential; poor prose can override scientific merit in editorial triage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt simple direct English and IMRAD layout. Use grammar/clarity tools, solicit colleague feedback, or use professional editing. Prepare an outline to ensure logical flow. Editors at top journals have little time; concise and clear manuscripts are prioritized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address ethical standards thoroughly on submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit, complete ethical and disclosure statements are required for editorial consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include IRB/ethical committee approvals and reference numbers, describe informed consent processes, and declare funding and conflicts of interest (or explicitly state none). Use a pre-submission checklist to confirm all required ethical documentation is present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame the study for broader relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Even local or small-sample studies should be presented in ways that highlight transferable lessons and wider implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare findings to international literature, discuss applicability to similar settings, and in the final Discussion paragraph connect results to larger policy, practice, or research trends. Emphasize generalizable insights rather than purely local facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be persistent and strategic after rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Desk rejection is common; authors should use it to improve and resubmit strategically rather than as a deterrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read rejection letters carefully for hints on improvements. Revise framing or target journal and resubmit without undue delay. Keep a submission tracker (Journal Name, Scope Fit, Status, Feedback, Next Steps) to manage momentum and learning across submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use available tools and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage journal-finder tools, reporting-guideline repositories, and capacity-building resources to strengthen submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Jane Journal Finder, Elsevier Journal Finder, Cofactor AuthorAID courses (for LMIC researchers), and the Equator Network for reporting guidelines. Use these to identify suitable journals, adhere to reporting standards, and improve manuscript quality.
